'''''Encephalartos horridus''''', commonly known as the '''Eastern Cape blue cycad''',<ref name="SANBI">{{Citation |last=Le Roux |first=Lou- Nita |title=Encephalartos horridus (Jacq.) Lehm |url=http://www.plantzafrica.com/plantefg/encephhorrid.htm |publisher=South African National Biodiversity Institute |date=April 2003 |access-date=2008-03-28 |archive-date=2016-11-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161107000230/http://www.plantzafrica.com/plantefg/encephhorrid.htm }}</ref> is a small, low-growing [[cycad]] up to {{convert|0.9|m|ft|abbr=on}} high and {{convert|0.9|m|ft|abbr=on}} wide.<ref name="ABC">{{Citation| last = Rodd | first = Tony | last2 = Bryant | first2 = Geoff | title = Flora's plantfinder: the right plants for every garden | place = Ultimo, NSW, Australia | publisher = ABC Books | year = 2007 | page = 905 | isbn = 978-0-7333-2094-1}}</ref> It is a native of [[Eastern Cape Province]], [[South Africa]], and found in arid shrublands, most commonly on ridges and slopes with shallow soils. The species is particularly known for its distinctly blue-gray leaves, although the degree of coloration can vary significantly.<ref name="plantnet">{{Citation |last=Hill |first=Ken |title=Encephalartos horridus |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/taxon.pl?name=Encephalartos+horridus |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney |access-date=2008-03-28}}</ref> The [[Binomial nomenclature|species name]] ''horridus'' is [[Latin]] for 'bristly', after the plant's stiff, spiny [[leaflet (botany)|leaflets]].<ref name=plantnet/>

==Description==
Mature plants have big stems of between {{convert|0.5|-|1|m|in|abbr=on}} in length and {{convert|20|-|30|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} in diameter<ref name="cycadsociety">{{Citation|title=Encephalartos horridus - (Jacq.) Lehmann |url=http://www.cycadsociety.org/horridus/horridus.html |publisher=The Cycad Society of South Africa |access-date=2008-03-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080511204500/http://www.cycadsociety.org/horridus/horridus.html |archive-date=2008-05-11 }}</ref> with the majority of the stem growing below ground.<ref name="ABC"/> Leaves are up to {{convert|1|m|in|abbr=on}} long and often sharply recurved towards the tip, looking stiff and spiny.<ref name=plantnet/> Younger leaves are a silvery-blue colour but turn green with age.<ref name="cycadsociety"/>

Cones are usually brownish- or blackish-red and single with a dense layer of fine hair. Both male and female cones are produced. The female cone is egg-shaped and up to {{convert|40|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|20|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} in diameter while the male cone is largely cylindrical narrowing towards the ends up to {{convert|40|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|12|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} in diameter. Seeds are roughly triangular with three flattened surfaces.<ref name="cycadsociety"/>

==Distribution==
Naturally occurring Eastern Cape blue cycads can only be found around Port Elizabeth and [[Uitenhage]] districts of Eastern Cape, South Africa, which has a warm climate year round, average annual rainfall in the range of {{convert|250|to|600|mm|in|abbr=on}} and summer temperatures up to {{convert|40|°C|°F|abbr=on}}.<ref name="cycadsociety" /> It prefers full sunlight and persists in a range of habitats including [[Karoo|Karoo scrub]], [[sourveld]], deep fertile soil and open rocky ridges.<ref name="cycadsociety"/>
In the wild there is evidence of distinct variation within the species, including a possible 'dwarf' form found around [[Port Elizabeth, Eastern Cape|Port Elizabeth]].<ref name="cycadsociety"/>

Eastern Cape blue cycads are now available as a result of commercial distribution in nurseries and gardens throughout the world.

==Ecology==
Cycads have few natural enemies; however, in the wild, they can be subject to predation from animals such as [[porcupine]]s, [[baboon]]s and certain [[insect]]s. Although the Eastern Cape blue cycad can reproduce by [[basal shoot|suckering]], more commonly reproduction requires insect pollination. Once seed cones have been pollinated seeds are spread by animals that eat the fleshy cones.<ref name=SANBI/>

==Conservation status==
This cycad is listed as an [[endangered species]] by the 2003 [[IUCN Red List]],<ref name="iucn status 18 November 2021" /> a change from its [[Vulnerable species|vulnerable]] listing in the 1997 IUCN Red List of Threatened Plants.<ref name=plantnet/> Historically it was over-collected in the wild but widespread availability in commercial nurseries has reduced some of this pressure.<ref name=SANBI/>

==Cultivation and propagation==
Like all cycads, the Eastern Cape blue cycad is a slow grower. It responds well to deep, fertile soil enriched with [[compost]].<ref name="cycadsociety"/> It is best suited to temperate and subtropical regions, however it can tolerate light to moderate frosts. It requires full sun, excellent drainage, not too much water and slightly acidic soil to prosper.<ref name="SANBI"/> It is common for the species to form new leaves and cones regularly.<ref name="cycadsociety"/> Plants are available from nurseries in many areas, however they are also easy to propagate from [[seed]]s.<ref name="cycadsociety"/> They can also be propagated from suckers with some patience and experience.<ref name="SANBI"/>
